title: Game Math: Vectors & Trig
blurb: The math behind movement: vectors, distances, angles, rotation, bouncing, homing missiles and a full physics tick.
intro:
Every moving thing in a game is math: a position, a velocity, a direction it's facing. This section teaches the handful of tools that power almost all 2D movement: vectors (an x and a y together), distance, the dot product, and the trig functions Math.cos, Math.sin and Math.atan2.

You'll write small helper functions that you could drop straight into a real game. Godot has these built in as Vector2 methods, and GameMaker has point_distance, lengthdir_x and friends. Here you'll build them yourself, so you'll know exactly what they do.

Tip

On screens, y grows downward. That means an angle of 90 degrees points down, not up. Every stage here uses screen coordinates.

stages.l:
A vector is just two numbers that belong together: an x and a y. It can mean a position (where something is) or a movement (which way and how far). In JavaScript, a small object is the easiest way to hold one.

const player = { x: 120, y: 80 };
console.log(player.x);   // 120
Tip

Shorthand: { x, y } means { x: x, y: y } when you already have variables with those names.
stages.p: Return a point object with properties x and y.
stages.h: return { x, y };

stages.l:
Adding two vectors means adding the x's and adding the y's. If a player is at (5, 5) and moves by (2, -1), they end up at (7, 4).

const pos = { x: 5, y: 5 };
const move = { x: 2, y: -1 };
const next = { x: pos.x + move.x, y: pos.y + move.y };   // { x: 7, y: 4 }
stages.p: Return a new vector that is a plus b.
stages.h: return { x: a.x + b.x, y: a.y + b.y };

stages.l:
Subtracting works the same way. The really useful part: target minus start gives the arrow pointing from start to target.

const enemy = { x: 2, y: 1 };
const player = { x: 5, y: 5 };
// arrow from enemy to player = player - enemy
// { x: 3, y: 4 }
stages.p: Return a minus b as a new vector.
stages.h: return { x: a.x - b.x, y: a.y - b.y };

stages.l:
Multiplying a vector by a plain number (called a scalar) stretches or shrinks it. Times 2 is twice as long, times 0.5 is half, times -1 points the opposite way.

// velocity of 4 pixels per frame, sped up by 1.5
const v = { x: 4, y: 0 };
const fast = { x: v.x * 1.5, y: v.y * 1.5 };   // { x: 6, y: 0 }
stages.p: Return v multiplied by the number k.
stages.h: Multiply both parts: { x: v.x * k, y: v.y * k }

stages.l:
The length (or magnitude) of a vector is how long the arrow is. It comes from Pythagoras: the x and y are the two short sides of a right triangle.

Math.sqrt(3 * 3 + 4 * 4);   // 5
Math.hypot(3, 4);           // 5, does the same thing

For a velocity, the length is the speed.
stages.p: Return the length of v.
stages.h: return Math.hypot(v.x, v.y);

stages.l:
A unit vector has length 1. It keeps only the direction. To normalize a vector, divide both parts by its length.

const v = { x: 3, y: 4 };      // length 5
const dir = { x: 3 / 5, y: 4 / 5 };   // { x: 0.6, y: 0.8 }

Why bother? Without it, a player holding right and down moves faster diagonally ((1, 1) has length 1.41). Normalize the input first, then multiply by the speed.

Tip

A zero vector has length 0, and dividing by 0 gives NaN. Always check for it.
stages.p: Return v as a unit vector. If v has length 0, return { x: 0, y: 0 }.
stages.h: const len = Math.hypot(v.x, v.y); Return the zero vector when len === 0, otherwise divide each part by len.

stages.l:
Put the last two ideas together: the distance between two points is the length of the arrow between them.

// distance = length of (b - a)

This one function answers loads of game questions: is the player close enough to pick up the coin, is the enemy in attack range, which tower is nearest?
stages.p: Return the distance between points a and b.
stages.h: return Math.hypot(b.x - a.x, b.y - a.y);

stages.l:
The dot product multiplies matching parts and adds them up: a.x * b.x + a.y * b.y. It sounds random, but it tells you how much two directions agree:

Dot productMeaning
positivepointing roughly the same way
zeroat right angles
negativepointing roughly opposite ways
stages.p: Return the dot product of a and b.
stages.h: return a.x * b.x + a.y * b.y;

stages.l:
Here's the dot product doing real work. A guard at pos faces direction facing. Is the player in front of them or behind?

Make the arrow from the guard to the target (target - pos), then dot it with facing. Positive means in front.

const toTarget = { x: target.x - pos.x, y: target.y - pos.y };
const d = facing.x * toTarget.x + facing.y * toTarget.y;
stages.p: Return true if target is in front of the guard (dot product greater than 0), otherwise false.
stages.h: Build toTarget as in the example, then return d > 0;

stages.l:
To aim a turret, you need the angle from it to the target. Math.atan2(dy, dx) gives it to you. Note the order: y first, then x.

Math.atan2(0, 1);    // 0, pointing right
Math.atan2(1, 0);    // 1.5707..., pointing down (screen y)
Math.atan2(0, -1);   // 3.14159..., pointing left

The answer is in radians, from -Math.PI to Math.PI. A full circle is 2 * Math.PI radians.
stages.p: Return the angle in radians from point from to point to.
stages.h: return Math.atan2(to.y - from.y, to.x - from.x);

stages.l:
Humans like degrees (360 in a circle). JavaScript's Math functions use radians (2 * Math.PI in a circle). Converting is one multiplication:

const toRad = deg => deg * Math.PI / 180;
const toDeg = rad => rad * 180 / Math.PI;
toRad(180);   // 3.14159...
DegreesRadians
90Math.PI / 2
180Math.PI
3602 * Math.PI
stages.p: Return the angle rad converted to degrees.
stages.h: return rad * 180 / Math.PI;

stages.l:
The reverse of atan2: you have an angle and want to move that way. Math.cos(angle) gives the x part of a unit arrow, and Math.sin(angle) gives the y part.

const angle = 30 * Math.PI / 180;   // radians!
const speed = 4;
bullet.x += Math.cos(angle) * speed;
bullet.y += Math.sin(angle) * speed;

This is exactly what GameMaker's lengthdir_x and lengthdir_y do.
stages.p: Return the new position after moving dist units from pos at deg degrees.
stages.h: Convert first: const a = deg * Math.PI / 180; then x: pos.x + Math.cos(a) * dist, and the same with sin for y.

stages.l:
To spin a point around the origin (0, 0) by angle a, use this formula. You don't need to memorise it, just know where to find it:

const c = Math.cos(a), s = Math.sin(a);
const rx = p.x * c - p.y * s;
const ry = p.x * s + p.y * c;

Games use this for spinning blades, orbiting moons, and turning the corners of a rotated sprite.
stages.p: Return point p rotated by deg degrees around (0, 0).
stages.h: Convert deg to radians, then use the two lines from the example.

stages.l:
Lerp (linear interpolation) finds a point part of the way from a to b. t = 0 is at a, t = 1 is at b, t = 0.5 is halfway.

const lerp = (a, b, t) => a + (b - a) * t;
lerp(0, 100, 0.25);   // 25

Lerping a camera a little toward the player each frame gives that smooth follow effect.
stages.p: Return the point a fraction t of the way from a to b.
stages.h: Lerp x and y separately: x: a.x + (b.x - a.x) * t

stages.l:
Movement in most games is two steps every frame:

  • Acceleration changes velocity (gravity pulls velocity downward).
  • Velocity changes position.

Multiply by dt (the seconds since the last frame) so the game runs the same speed on fast and slow computers.

body.vy += body.ay * dt;   // 1. speed up
body.y  += body.vy * dt;   // 2. move

Update velocity first, then position. This order is called semi-implicit Euler and it's what most game engines use.
stages.p: Return a new body after one step of dt seconds. Keep ax and ay the same.
stages.h: Work out vx and vy first, then x: body.x + vx * dt using the new velocity. Return all six properties.

stages.l:
Two circles touch when the distance between their centres is no more than their two radii added together. It's the cheapest collision check there is, so lots of games use circles for bullets and enemies even when the sprites aren't round.

const d = Math.hypot(b.x - a.x, b.y - a.y);
const hit = d <= a.r + b.r;
Tip

For speed, skip the square root: compare dx * dx + dy * dy with (a.r + b.r) ** 2. Same answer, no Math.sqrt.
stages.p: Each circle is { x, y, r }. Return true if they overlap or just touch.
stages.h: return Math.hypot(b.x - a.x, b.y - a.y) <= a.r + b.r;

stages.l:
A wall's normal is a unit vector sticking straight out of it. To bounce a velocity v off a wall with normal n, use:

// reflected = v - 2 * dot(v, n) * n
const d = v.x * n.x + v.y * n.y;
const rx = v.x - 2 * d * n.x;
const ry = v.y - 2 * d * n.y;

For a floor (normal pointing up, (0, -1)) this just flips vy, but it works for walls at any angle, like the slanted bumpers in a pinball table.
stages.p: Return velocity v reflected off a wall with unit normal n.
stages.h: Work out d (the dot product) first, then subtract 2 * d * n.x from v.x and the same for y.

stages.l:
A homing missile shouldn't snap to face its target. It turns a little each frame, up to maxTurn degrees. The tricky part is going the short way round: from 10 degrees to 350, you should turn 20 degrees left, not 340 right.

This line wraps any difference into the range -180 to 180:

const diff = ((target - angle) % 360 + 540) % 360 - 180;

Then clamp it to the turn limit, add it on, and wrap the result back into 0 to 360:

const turn = Math.max(-maxTurn, Math.min(maxTurn, diff));
const next = ((angle + turn) % 360 + 360) % 360;
stages.p: All angles are in degrees from 0 to 360. Return the missile's new angle after turning toward target by at most maxTurn, the short way round.
stages.h: Combine the two snippets from the lesson and return next.

stages.l:
Stealth games give guards a view cone: a range and a field of view. A target is seen if it's close enough and the angle to it is within half the field of view of where the guard is facing.

const deg = Math.atan2(dy, dx) * 180 / Math.PI;     // angle to target
const diff = ((deg - facing) % 360 + 540) % 360 - 180; // short way round
const inCone = Math.abs(diff) <= fov / 2;
stages.p: guard is { x, y, facing, fov, range } with angles in degrees. Return true if target is within range and inside the view cone.
stages.h: Check the distance first: if Math.hypot(dx, dy) > guard.range return false. Then use the angle check from the lesson.

stages.l:
Time to fly. This is one frame of an Asteroids-style ship, using almost everything from this section. Each tick does four things, in order:

  • Turn: add input.turn * TURN_SPEED * dt to the angle (turn is -1, 0 or 1), then wrap it into 0 to 360.
  • Thrust: if input.thrust is true, add THRUST * dt to the velocity in the direction the ship faces.
  • Speed limit: if the speed is more than MAX_SPEED, scale the velocity down so its length is exactly MAX_SPEED.
  • Move: add velocity * dt to the position.
const TURN_SPEED = 180;   // degrees per second
const THRUST = 100;       // speed gained per second
const MAX_SPEED = 200;
stages.p: Return the ship { x, y, vx, vy, angle } after one tick of dt seconds, following the four steps.
stages.h: For the speed limit: const speed = Math.hypot(vx, vy); and if it's too big, multiply both vx and vy by MAX_SPEED / speed. Remember cos and sin need radians.
